Read any procedure written in English and you will notice that almost nobody is in it. The order is received. The invoice is checked. The shipment is released. Somebody does each of those things, of course, and the document simply does not care which person it was, because the procedure has to work on a Tuesday when three of them are on holiday. That is what the structure is for. It moves the action to the front and lets the person disappear, and in a manual that is exactly right. The trouble starts when the same structure walks out of the manual and into a conversation. Mistakes were made is a famous sentence for a reason. The grammar has not changed at all, and what it does has changed completely: in a procedure it removes noise, and in an apology it removes the person who owes you one.

I sent a status report once that I was quite pleased with. Everything in it was true and every line was in the passive. The dates had been reviewed, the risks had been identified, the supplier had been contacted. My manager read it in about forty seconds and asked me one question. Who. Not what, not when. Who. And I could not answer half of it, because I had written the report from a list of things that had happened rather than from a list of people doing them, and the two are not the same document at all. What I learned that day is a rule I still use. Write it in the passive if you want, and then read it back and put a name in front of every line, silently, for yourself. Any line where you cannot is a line where nobody is actually doing the work.
